Academic Identity and Professional Development

In: Higher Education Beyond Boundaries: Dynamics, Change, Challenges and Opportunities

Meenu Rani and Amman Jakhar

[Affiliations] · Corresponding author: [name, e-mail]

Keywords: academic identity; continuous professional development; faculty development; mentoring; communities of practice; digital pedagogy; artificial intelligence in education; micro-credentials; academic resilience; well-being; institutional excellence

Abstract

Academic identity in contemporary higher education is no longer a stable, discipline-anchored self-understanding. It is a provisional configuration that academics assemble and reassemble across teaching, research, leadership, community engagement and lifelong learning. This chapter theorises academic identity as a fluid, relational and negotiated construct. It is shaped at the micro level by personal values and self-efficacy, at the meso level by disciplinary communities and institutional cultures, and at the macro level by national policy regimes, global competition, digitalisation and interdisciplinarity. Drawing on scholarship in the sociology of higher education, teacher identity research and organisational psychology, the chapter makes four arguments.

  1. Identity formation is a continuous negotiation between personal aspiration and systemic pressure, mediated by performance appraisal, workload allocation and reward structures.
  2. Continuous professional development is most effective when it is organised as an integrated ecosystem. Such an ecosystem combines faculty development programmes, mentoring, collaborative learning communities, digital pedagogy, research capacity building and leadership development, and increasingly competency-based learning, AI-supported teaching and micro-credentialing.
  3. Workload intensification, metric-driven accountability, career insecurity and the demands of digital adaptation threaten professional well-being. These threats can be explained with the job demands–resources model and addressed through resilience, reflective practice, inclusive leadership and institutional well-being policy.
  4. Institutions sustain academic identity only when they act as guarantors of academic freedom, ethical scholarship and fair career progression.

Four conceptual figures and four analytical tables summarise the frameworks. The chapter concludes that sustained, institutionally embedded professional learning is the principal mechanism through which academic identity and institutional transformation can be aligned in a higher education system that increasingly operates beyond national, disciplinary and modal boundaries.

Introduction

Few occupational identities have been subjected to as sustained a reconfiguration over the past three decades as that of the university academic. The traditional image of the academic was a disciplinary expert whose authority rested on research, whose teaching followed from scholarship, and whose loyalty lay primarily with a community of peers. This image has been unsettled by the massification of higher education, the rise of managerial governance, the digitisation of teaching and research, and the integration of national systems into global markets for students, talent and prestige. Henkel's analysis of academics working through successive waves of policy reform showed that identity is constructed within disciplinary and institutional communities that themselves change under policy pressure, rather than being simply carried by individuals [1]. Barnett has argued that universities now operate in conditions of "supercomplexity", in which the frameworks used to interpret academic work are multiple, contested and continually revised [2]. Under such conditions, academic identity becomes an ongoing accomplishment rather than a settled possession.

This chapter examines the implications of this shift for the professional lives and development of university teachers. It is organised in four sections that move from diagnosis to prescription. Section 1 establishes the fluid nature of academic identity and analyses the institutional and external forces that shape it. Section 2 examines the pathways through which continuous professional development (CPD) can support identity formation and professional excellence, including emerging competencies and future-oriented modes of learning. Section 3 critically analyses the systemic pressures that threaten academic careers and well-being and sets out strategies for resilience. Section 4 considers the institution's responsibility as a source of innovation and ethical scholarship, and argues that sustained professional learning is the key to aligning individual identity with institutional transformation.

Throughout, the chapter draws on international scholarship while attending to the Indian policy context, in which the National Education Policy 2020 and the regulatory framework of the University Grants Commission are reshaping expectations of faculty. The analysis is conceptual and integrative rather than empirical. Its aim is to provide a theoretically grounded framework that researchers can test, and that academic developers and institutional leaders can use to design and evaluate interventions.

Section 1: The Shifting Landscape of Academic Identity

1.1 The Fluid Nature of Academic Identity

Identity, in the sense used in this chapter, refers to the reflexive understanding that individuals hold of who they are as professionals. It includes the values they hold, the practices they recognise as their own, the communities to which they belong, and the futures they imagine for themselves. Clegg's study of academics in a UK university showed that, contrary to narratives of loss and decline, academics actively construct identities from a wide repertoire of resources. These include personal histories, political commitments, disciplinary attachments and institutional roles, and identity is "threatened" only when these resources are foreclosed [3]. This perspective shifts the analytical focus from the erosion of a single, authentic academic self to the conditions under which multiple, overlapping identities can be sustained.

The disciplinary community has traditionally been the primary anchor of academic identity. Becher and Trowler's account of "academic tribes and territories" demonstrated that disciplines carry distinctive epistemologies, communicative norms and reward structures that socialise their members into recognisable ways of being an academic [4]. Disciplinary belonging remains important, but it is now one anchor among several. Research on professional identity in teaching has emphasised that identity is an ongoing process of interpretation and reinterpretation of experience. It involves both person and context, consists of sub-identities that may be more or less harmonious, and depends on agency [5]. Applied to higher education, this suggests that teaching, research, leadership and engagement roles can each support distinct sub-identities, whose integration is a professional achievement rather than a given.

Wenger's social theory of learning provides a useful mechanism for understanding how such integration occurs [6]. In this account, identity is formed through participation in communities of practice: through engagement in shared activity, imagination of oneself in relation to a broader world, and alignment with the purposes of a larger enterprise. Because academics participate simultaneously in disciplinary, departmental, institutional, professional and international communities, their identities are constituted at the nexus of multi-membership. Each boundary crossing is an occasion for learning and for identity work. This conceptualisation explains why identity is inherently dynamic. Every change in the configuration of communities, such as a new interdisciplinary research centre, a shift to online teaching or a leadership appointment, requires academics to renegotiate the meaning of their work.

The expansion of what counts as legitimate academic work has reinforced this multiplicity. Boyer's influential reconceptualisation of scholarship identified four interrelated forms: discovery, integration, application and teaching [7]. It thereby legitimated identities grounded in pedagogy, synthesis and engagement alongside those grounded in original research. At the same time, the boundaries between academic and professional roles have become increasingly porous. Whitchurch identified the emergence of "third space" professionals who work across academic and administrative domains, in roles such as educational development, research management and community partnership. These roles combine the credentials and orientations of both, and their holders develop hybrid identities that do not fit traditional categories [8]. Such roles are no longer marginal. They are often where institutional innovation is concentrated.

Teaching identity deserves particular attention. Kreber argued that authenticity in university teaching involves more than technical competence. It requires a critical, self-reflective engagement with one's values, with the interests of students and with the purposes of higher education [9]. From this perspective, teaching identity is a moral as well as a professional project. It is developed through reflection on why one teaches as one does, in addition to how. This has direct implications for professional development, which must address values and purposes as well as skills.

Three macro-level transformations intensify the fluidity of academic identity. The first is globalisation and internationalisation. Altbach and Knight showed that internationalisation is driven by a combination of academic, economic, political and cultural motives, and that it has profoundly altered the mobility of students and staff, the organisation of research collaboration and the competitive positioning of institutions [10]. For individual academics, internationalisation brings both opportunity and pressure. It offers access to global networks and audiences, and it exposes academics to international benchmarks of productivity and prestige.

The second transformation is digitalisation. Selwyn has cautioned against technologically determinist accounts of the "digital university". He showed instead that digital technologies are entangled with institutional politics, commercial interests and longstanding pedagogical debates, and that they reconfigure rather than simply enhance academic labour [11]. Digital platforms change how teaching is designed and delivered, how research is conducted and disseminated, and how academic performance is monitored. Each of these changes implies a renegotiation of professional roles.

The third transformation is the rise of interdisciplinarity. Complex societal problems in health, climate, technology and development increasingly require knowledge that transcends single disciplines. Academics who work across disciplinary boundaries must reconcile divergent epistemic norms. Their contributions are often harder to recognise in disciplinary evaluation regimes, so the tension between disciplinary belonging and problem-oriented collaboration becomes a significant source of identity work.

Figure 1 integrates these arguments into a multidimensional model of academic identity. Five role domains form overlapping fields around a negotiated core: teaching, research, leadership, community engagement and lifelong learning. The overlaps represent hybrid identities, such as the scholar of teaching and learning or the engaged researcher. The three macro-level transformations continuously reshape the relative weight and configuration of the domains. The foundational argument of this subsection follows from this analysis. In a system characterised by supercomplexity, flexibility in knowledge, skills and professional roles is an essential condition of academic effectiveness, not an optional disposition. Flexibility here does not mean the dissolution of commitment. Rather, it denotes the capacity to hold multiple sub-identities in productive tension, to cross boundaries between communities without losing a coherent professional purpose, and to treat change as an occasion for learning. Professional development, as argued in Section 2, is the principal institutional means of cultivating this capacity.

1.2 Institutional and External Forces Shaping Identity

If academic identity is fluid, it is not freely chosen. Academics construct their identities within structures that allocate time, recognition and resources, and that define what counts as valuable work. Henkel's later analysis of academic autonomy showed how policy changes have reconfigured the boundaries between the academy, the state and the market. Autonomy is increasingly understood less as freedom from external control and more as the capacity to manage multiple stakeholder demands [12]. Academic identity is thus formed at the intersection of individual agency and institutional structuring, and its analysis requires attention to both.

Institutional culture is the first and most proximate structuring force. Institutions differ in mission, in the relative weight they attach to teaching and research, in their governance arrangements and in the informal norms that shape everyday academic life. A research-intensive university, a teaching-focused college and a professional institute will socialise their staff into different conceptions of the good academic. Even within a single institution, departmental cultures mediate institutional priorities, filtering and reinterpreting them through local disciplinary norms.

Performance appraisal and reward systems are the second force, and arguably the most consequential. Ball's analysis of performativity remains a powerful account of how measurement regimes reshape professional subjectivity [13]. When professional worth is represented through indicators, targets and comparisons, practitioners come to experience their work in terms of what can be measured. This produces a split between the authentic purposes of their practice and the performances required for accountability. Ball described the resulting condition as one of ontological insecurity, in which professionals are unsure whether they are doing enough, or doing the right thing, because judgement has been externalised to metrics. Shore and Wright extended this analysis to the global level. They showed how rankings and ratings have become technologies of governance that reorder institutions and individuals according to standardised comparisons [14]. For academics, such audit cultures transform identity from an expression of scholarly commitment into a portfolio to be optimised.

National educational policy is the third structuring force. In India, the National Education Policy 2020 envisages a large-scale transformation of higher education. It envisages multidisciplinary institutions, flexible curricula with multiple entry and exit points, the integration of vocational and academic learning, increased use of technology, and greater emphasis on research through a national research foundation [15]. The policy explicitly identifies faculty as central to this transformation. It calls for motivated, energised and capable faculty, for continuous professional development, and for merit-based career management. These aspirations redefine the expected identity of the Indian academic in multidisciplinary, research-active, technologically capable and student-centred terms. Realising them, however, depends on institutional capacity and on the alignment of incentives.

Career advancement in Indian universities and colleges is governed by the University Grants Commission's 2018 regulations on minimum qualifications and the maintenance of standards. These regulations set out criteria for recruitment and promotion that combine teaching, research outputs, participation in orientation and refresher programmes, and other academic contributions [16]. Regulatory frameworks of this kind are not neutral. By specifying which activities count toward promotion and how they are weighted, they signal which identities are institutionally valued. Where publication counts dominate, teaching innovation and community engagement may be undervalued. Where participation in professional development is a formal requirement, it risks becoming a compliance exercise rather than a vehicle for growth.

Changing employment structures are a fourth force. Kezar and Sam documented the growth of non-tenure-track and contingent academic appointments in the United States. Such appointments now constitute the majority of the academic workforce and are associated with reduced job security, limited access to professional development and exclusion from governance [17]. Comparable patterns of fixed-term, guest and contractual appointments exist in many systems, including India. They fragment the academic profession into those with secure, multidimensional roles and those whose identities are constrained to narrowly defined teaching functions. They also make the development of a coherent professional identity contingent on contractual status.

Technological innovation and changing student expectations constitute the fifth and sixth forces. Learning management systems, plagiarism-detection tools, learning analytics and, most recently, generative artificial intelligence alter the visibility and the nature of academic work. Students who have grown up with digital media expect flexibility, responsiveness and relevance, and frequently approach higher education as an investment in employability. These expectations press academics to redefine their role from transmitters of knowledge to designers of learning experiences, mentors and facilitators. Many academics welcome this redefinition, while others experience it as a dilution of disciplinary expertise.

The interaction of these forces is especially visible in systems undergoing rapid policy change. In the Indian case, the National Education Policy 2020 asks academics to adopt multidisciplinary, research-active and technology-enabled identities [15]. At the same time, promotion continues to be governed by codified criteria that weight particular outputs [16], and a significant share of teaching is delivered by staff on temporary or contractual terms. Academics in such settings experience competing signals. Policy rhetoric invites experimentation and breadth, appraisal rewards measurable outputs, and employment conditions may preclude long-term investment in development. Identity work under these conditions is a form of strategic sense-making. Academics interpret which expectations are binding, which are aspirational and which can safely be ignored, and they construct professional selves that are viable within the resulting configuration [3,12].

Figure 2 represents these forces as a nested ecological system. The individual academic is located at the centre, embedded in disciplinary and departmental communities, institutional cultures, national policy and regulation, and the global environment. Top-down structuring flows inward from each layer, while bottom-up agency flows outward. The interaction between the two produces a range of identity outcomes. Academics may align with institutional expectations, comply strategically while preserving a private sense of purpose, resist, reinvent themselves in hybrid roles, or exit the profession. The model frames identity formation as a negotiation between personal aspirations and systemic pressures, consistent with the analyses of Henkel, Clegg and Ball [3,12,13]. It also highlights the levers through which institutions can widen or narrow the space for agency. As Figure 2 indicates, these levers are located at every level of the system, not only within the institution.

Section 2: Pathways for Continuous Professional Development

2.1 Faculty Development, Mentoring, and Collaborative Learning

Continuous professional development refers to the planned and sustained processes through which academics extend their knowledge, skills, values and professional judgement throughout their careers. In higher education, CPD has historically been organised under the label of faculty development or educational development. Sorcinelli and colleagues traced the evolution of the field through successive ages. It began with an early focus on the scholar, in which development meant support for research. It moved through the teacher and the developer, and arrived at the networker, in which development is understood as a collaborative, institution-wide enterprise connected to strategic priorities [18]. Their analysis also identified the challenges that faculty development must now address: the changing nature of the professoriate, the diversity of students, the pressures of assessment and accountability, and the transformation of pedagogy by technology.

The evidence on the effectiveness of formal faculty development programmes is encouraging but nuanced. Steinert and colleagues' systematic review of faculty development initiatives in medical education found high satisfaction with programmes. It also found positive changes in participants' attitudes toward teaching, gains in knowledge and skills, and changes in teaching behaviour, with some evidence of impact on students and organisations [19]. The review identified the features associated with effectiveness: experiential learning, provision of feedback, effective peer and colleague relationships, intentional design based on principles of teaching and learning, and the use of multiple instructional methods within a single intervention. Stes and colleagues' review of instructional development in higher education reached complementary conclusions [20]. Initiatives extended over time had more impact than one-off workshops. Impact on teachers' behaviour and on student learning was less frequently studied, and more difficult to demonstrate, than impact on teachers' attitudes and conceptions. Together these reviews suggest that faculty development is most effective when it is sustained, practice-based and collegial.

Research on teacher professional development in the school sector provides a well-validated framework for these conclusions. Desimone proposed a core conceptual framework identifying five features of effective professional development [21]:

  • content focus;
  • active learning;
  • coherence with teachers' knowledge, beliefs and institutional priorities;
  • sufficient duration;
  • collective participation.

Darling-Hammond and colleagues' synthesis of rigorous studies extended this framework. They added the use of models of effective practice, coaching and expert support, and opportunities for feedback and reflection [22]. Although these frameworks were developed for school teachers, their emphasis on sustained, collaborative, practice-embedded learning transfers well to higher education. University teachers, like school teachers, learn most effectively when development is situated in their own practice and shared with colleagues.

The evaluation of CPD deserves explicit attention, because what institutions measure shapes what they value. Desimone's framework proposes a causal chain [21]. Professional development first changes teachers' knowledge, skills, attitudes and beliefs. These changes alter instructional practice, and changes in practice in turn improve student learning. Contextual factors such as institutional leadership and policy moderate each link in the chain. Most institutional evaluations of faculty development stop at the first link, measuring satisfaction and self-reported learning. The reviews by Steinert and colleagues and by Stes and colleagues both identified a shortage of evidence on behavioural change and on student outcomes [19,20]. A more rigorous evaluation culture would combine participant feedback with observation of practice, analysis of teaching materials and student learning data, and longitudinal follow-up. It would also treat evaluation as an opportunity for collective reflection rather than as an exercise in accountability.

Mentoring is the second major mechanism. Kram's foundational study of developmental relationships in organisations distinguished between the career functions of mentoring and its psychosocial functions [23]. Career functions include sponsorship, exposure, coaching, protection and challenging assignments. Psychosocial functions include role modelling, acceptance, counselling and friendship. Both are directly relevant to academic identity. Career functions help early-career academics navigate tacit institutional rules on publication, grant writing and promotion. Psychosocial functions support the development of professional confidence and a sense of belonging. Contemporary models of academic mentoring have moved beyond the traditional dyad of senior and junior colleague toward mentoring constellations. These include peer mentoring, group mentoring, reverse mentoring in digital skills, and cross-institutional and international mentoring networks. Such diversified models are particularly valuable for academics from groups under-represented in senior positions, who may lack access to informal sponsorship.

Collaborative learning communities are the third mechanism. Cox defined faculty learning communities as cross-disciplinary groups of academics and staff who engage in an active, collaborative, year-long programme. The programme has a curriculum focused on enhancing teaching and learning, and involves frequent seminars and activities that provide learning, development, scholarship and community building [24]. Faculty learning communities give institutional form to Wenger's concept of communities of practice. They create protected spaces in which academics can experiment with new practices, reflect on their experience and develop shared repertoires. Cox's account also emphasises that such communities address the isolation that many academics experience in teaching, which has traditionally been a private activity conducted behind closed classroom doors.

Three domains of development form the core pillars of a contemporary CPD system.

Digital pedagogy. Mishra and Koehler's framework of technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) holds that effective technology integration requires an understanding of the interactions between technology, pedagogy and content, rather than technical skill alone [25]. Development in digital pedagogy should therefore be discipline-sensitive and pedagogically grounded, not tool-centred.

Research capacity building. This includes training in research methods and ethics, support for grant writing and publication, participation in research networks and the development of doctoral supervision skills. It is particularly important in institutions and systems undergoing a transition toward research intensity, as envisaged for Indian higher education.

Leadership development. This prepares academics for programme, departmental and institutional leadership. It emphasises collegial, inclusive and change-oriented approaches rather than purely managerial competences.

Figure 3 presents an integrated CPD ecosystem that links these mechanisms and pillars. Development proceeds through a cycle of five stages:

  1. needs diagnosis;
  2. engagement with learning pathways;
  3. integration into practice;
  4. evidence and recognition;
  5. career progression.

Reflective practice and evaluation feed back into the next cycle. The four pillars of digital pedagogy, research capacity, leadership development and collegial infrastructure sustain the cycle. Institutional enabling conditions underpin all of them: policy alignment, resources, and an ethical and inclusive culture. Table 2 compares the principal mechanisms of CPD in terms of their focus, mode, strengths, limitations and evidence base, providing a basis for selecting and combining them.

2.2 Emerging Competencies and Future-Oriented Learning

The competencies required of academics are expanding rapidly. Four domains of emerging competency are particularly salient: online pedagogy, AI-supported education, interdisciplinary knowledge and cross-border academic mobility. Each requires not only new skills but also new ways of understanding the academic role.

Online pedagogy became a universal requirement almost overnight during the COVID-19 pandemic, when institutions worldwide shifted to remote teaching. Hodges and colleagues distinguished between "emergency remote teaching", a temporary shift of instructional delivery to remote modes in response to crisis, and online learning proper [26]. Online learning is the product of careful instructional design and planning, using systematic models for course development. The distinction matters for professional development. The rapid, improvised adaptation of 2020 demonstrated academics' capacity for flexibility. It did not in itself constitute the development of expertise in online pedagogy, which requires understanding of learning design, interaction, assessment and learner support in digital environments. Post-pandemic professional development must therefore move from emergency adaptation toward systematic, research-informed capability in online and blended learning.

Artificial intelligence presents a still more profound challenge. Zawacki-Richter and colleagues' systematic review of research on AI applications in higher education identified four main areas of application: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems [27]. The review also observed that the literature showed weak connection to pedagogical theory and a lack of critical reflection on ethical risks, and it asked pointedly: "where are the educators?" Since that review, generative AI has made these questions urgent. UNESCO's guidance on generative AI in education and research calls for a human-centred approach [28]. It recommends that institutions validate the ethical and pedagogical appropriateness of AI tools, protect data privacy, and build the capacity of teachers and researchers to use AI critically and responsibly. For academic identity, AI raises fundamental questions. They concern the nature of expertise when information synthesis is automated, the integrity of assessment, the authorship of scholarly work, and the distinctive human contribution of the teacher. AI literacy for academics therefore encompasses technical familiarity, pedagogical design, critical evaluation of outputs and biases, ethical reasoning and policy awareness.

Interdisciplinary knowledge is a third emerging competency. It is driven by the complexity of societal problems and by policy commitments to multidisciplinary education, including those in the National Education Policy 2020 [15]. Interdisciplinary competence involves the ability to understand the epistemic assumptions of other disciplines, to communicate across disciplinary languages, to integrate methods and insights, and to collaborate in teams with diverse expertise. Developing this competence requires structured opportunities for cross-disciplinary engagement, which faculty learning communities and interdisciplinary research centres can provide [24].

Cross-border academic mobility is the fourth domain. It includes physical mobility for teaching, research and study, and increasingly virtual mobility through collaborative online international learning and international research networks [10]. Mobility develops intercultural competence, extends professional networks and exposes academics to alternative pedagogical and research cultures. Global research networks enable participation in large-scale, multi-site research that no single institution could sustain. For academics in institutions with limited resources, virtual networks offer a relatively accessible route to international engagement.

Several emerging developments in professional learning respond to these competency demands. Competency-based professional learning organises development around explicitly defined competencies rather than seat time or course completion. Academics demonstrate attainment through evidence of practice, such as teaching portfolios, peer observation, designed learning materials and research outputs. This approach aligns development with the integrated professional standards now used in many systems. It also allows academics to pursue personalised pathways according to career stage and role.

Micro-credentialing provides a mechanism for recognising such learning in granular, portable units. The OECD's analysis of micro-credential innovations described micro-credentials as short, focused learning experiences with certified outcomes. It noted their potential to support flexible, lifelong learning, while also identifying challenges of quality assurance, recognition and transparency [29]. The Council of the European Union's 2022 recommendation set out a common definition and standard elements for micro-credentials, together with principles for their design and issuance [30]. The standard elements include learning outcomes, workload, level, assessment and quality assurance. For faculty development, micro-credentials make it possible to recognise specific competencies, for example in online assessment design, AI-supported feedback or research data management. They can be stacked toward larger qualifications and recognised across institutions and borders. Their value depends on rigorous quality assurance and on their integration into career-advancement frameworks, so that they do not become a new form of credentialism.

AI support for teaching is itself an avenue for professional learning. AI tools can assist academics in designing learning materials, generating formative feedback, analysing student engagement and personalising support. Used critically, they can free time for higher-order pedagogical work and for the relational dimensions of teaching that remain distinctively human. The professional learning required is therefore twofold. Academics must learn to use AI tools effectively, and they must learn to judge when and how such tools serve, or undermine, educational purposes [27,28].

Table 3 sets out a framework of emerging competencies for future-ready academic practice. It specifies key capabilities, development pathways, illustrative micro-credentials and indicators of attainment for each domain. The framework is intended as a design tool for institutions developing competency-based CPD. It can be mapped onto the development cycle shown in Figure 3, in which micro-credentials function as the recognition mechanism at stage four.

Section 3: Challenges and Critiques in Academic Professional Life

3.1 Navigating Systemic Pressures and Career Insecurity

The expansion of academic roles and competencies described in the preceding sections has a darker counterpart. Each new expectation, whether to teach online, to integrate AI, to publish internationally, to secure external funding, to engage communities or to acquire new credentials, is typically added to existing responsibilities rather than substituted for them. The result is a structural intensification of academic work. This subsection analyses the principal systemic pressures that threaten professional well-being and the sustainability of academic careers.

Workload is the most pervasive pressure. Kinman and Wray's survey of staff in UK higher education reported high levels of occupational stress [31]. It identified excessive demands, low control over work, insufficient support and poor work–life balance as key concerns, and these were linked to long working hours. Although the specific findings relate to one national system, the underlying dynamics are widely reported internationally. These dynamics are expanding student numbers, increased administrative and reporting requirements, and the extension of work into evenings and weekends through digital connectivity. Workload pressures are often compounded by opaque workload allocation models that fail to capture the full range of academic activity, particularly pastoral care, curriculum development and service.

Research productivity demands constitute a second pressure. In audit cultures, research performance is increasingly represented through quantitative indicators: publication counts, journal impact factors, citation indices and grant income [14]. These indicators feed into individual appraisal, institutional rankings and funding allocations. They create incentives for academics to prioritise quantity over quality, to fragment research into minimal publishable units, and to favour topics and venues that maximise measurable output. In some contexts these incentives have contributed to the proliferation of predatory publishing and other threats to research integrity. Productivity pressures also fall unevenly. They disadvantage academics with heavy teaching loads, those in under-resourced institutions, and those with caring responsibilities that limit discretionary research time.

Career insecurity is a third pressure. As discussed in Section 1.2, the growth of contingent appointments has created a stratified profession in which a substantial proportion of academics work on fixed-term, part-time or hourly contracts [17]. Contingent academics frequently experience low pay, exclusion from governance and professional development, and limited prospects of advancement. These conditions make it difficult to sustain a coherent academic identity or to plan a career. Insecurity also affects early-career academics on permanent pathways, for whom probation, promotion criteria and competition for scarce positions generate sustained anxiety.

These pressures are not distributed evenly across the academic workforce. Early-career academics and staff on contingent contracts face the combination of high demands and low resources that the job demands–resources literature associates with the greatest risk of strain [17,32]. Academics with caring responsibilities, who are disproportionately women, have less discretionary time for the research activity that dominates appraisal. Academics in under-resourced institutions face international productivity benchmarks without access to comparable infrastructure, funding or research support. An analysis of systemic pressures that ignores these inequalities risks treating the experience of the most secure and well-resourced academics as the norm. A professional development strategy designed on that basis would tend to widen rather than narrow existing disparities.

Gill's analysis of the "hidden injuries" of neoliberal academia provides a powerful interpretive frame for these pressures [33]. Gill argued that the experiences of exhaustion, stress, insecurity, shame and feelings of fraudulence widely reported by academics are not individual pathologies. They are structural products of neoliberal governance. These experiences are frequently silenced because they conflict with the image of the passionate, self-directed academic who loves their work. The very commitment that draws academics to the profession is thus mobilised to secure their compliance with intensified demands. This analysis complements Ball's account of performativity [13]. Together they reveal how systemic pressures are internalised as personal responsibility.

Adaptation to the digital world constitutes a fourth pressure. It is closely related to workload but has distinctive features. Digital technologies extend the reach and visibility of academic work, but they also erode boundaries between work and private life, create expectations of constant availability, and require continuous learning as platforms and tools change [11]. The emergence of generative AI adds new demands. Academics must redesign assessments, develop policies on acceptable use, and engage with students' AI-mediated learning, often without adequate institutional guidance or time [28].

The job demands–resources (JD-R) model provides an integrative explanation of how these pressures affect well-being [32]. The model distinguishes between job demands and job resources. Job demands are the physical, psychological, social or organisational aspects of a job that require sustained effort and are therefore associated with physiological and psychological costs. Job resources are aspects of a job that are functional in achieving work goals, reduce job demands or stimulate personal growth and development. The model proposes two processes:

  1. a health-impairment process, in which chronic demands deplete energy and lead to exhaustion and health problems;
  2. a motivational process, in which resources foster engagement and performance.

Resources can buffer the impact of demands. Applied to academic work, the JD-R model explains why the same demands can lead to burnout for some academics and to growth for others. The difference lies in the resources available to them, including autonomy, collegial support, development opportunities, fair appraisal and personal resources such as self-efficacy. The policy implication is that reducing demands and increasing resources are complementary strategies. Institutions that add demands without commensurate resources should expect strain, disengagement and attrition.

3.2 Strategies for Academic Resilience and Well-Being

Recognising that the pressures described above are structural does not imply that individual and collective responses are futile. On the contrary, the JD-R model and research on resilience both suggest that strategic interventions at multiple levels can shift the balance from the health-impairment process toward the motivational process. This subsection outlines four strategies: academic resilience, reflective practice, inclusive leadership and institutional well-being initiatives.

Academic resilience is the capacity to sustain professional commitment and effectiveness in the face of adversity. Gu and Day's research on teachers' resilience reconceptualised it as a relative, dynamic and developmental construct, not a fixed personal trait [34]. It emerges from the interaction between individual dispositions and the professional and organisational contexts in which teachers work. Resilience in this sense is relational. It is nurtured by supportive leadership, collegial relationships and a sense of moral purpose, and it is eroded by isolation and adverse working conditions. This conceptualisation has two important implications. First, resilience can be developed and is therefore a legitimate focus for professional development. Second, responsibility for resilience is shared between individuals and institutions. Framing resilience as an individual obligation risks reproducing the dynamic Gill identified, in which structural problems are converted into personal deficits [33].

Reflective practice is a second strategy. It is closely connected to resilience and to identity. Schön's account of the reflective practitioner challenged the model of technical rationality, in which professional practice is the application of scientific theory to instrumental problems [35]. Schön showed instead that competent practitioners engage in reflection-in-action, a tacit, improvisational inquiry conducted in the midst of practice, and in reflection-on-action, a retrospective analysis of experience. For academics, reflective practice serves several functions. It supports the continuous improvement of teaching and research. It enables critical examination of the values and assumptions embedded in practice, which is central to authentic teaching identity [9]. It also provides a means of making sense of, and responding to, the tensions created by systemic pressures. Reflective practice can be cultivated through teaching portfolios, reflective journals, peer observation and dialogue, and the collaborative inquiry of learning communities [24].

Inclusive leadership is a third strategy. Academic leaders at programme, departmental and institutional levels shape the conditions under which academics work, the distribution of workload and recognition, and the climate of collegiality. Inclusive leadership values diverse contributions, distributes leadership responsibility, makes decisions transparently and attends to the well-being of colleagues. It can mitigate many of the pressures described above. Leaders can implement transparent and equitable workload models, recognise teaching, engagement and service alongside research, and protect time for development. They can also model sustainable working practices and create conditions of psychological safety in which colleagues can raise concerns without fear. Leadership development, identified in Section 2.1 as a core pillar of CPD, is therefore also a well-being intervention.

Institutional well-being initiatives constitute the fourth strategy. They operate at the level of policy and structure. Self-determination theory offers a valuable framework for designing such initiatives [36]. It holds that well-being and intrinsic motivation depend on the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. Institutional policies can support autonomy by preserving academic freedom and discretion over work. They can support competence through development opportunities and constructive feedback, and relatedness through collegial structures and inclusive cultures. Conversely, policies that rely on controlling forms of accountability, provide inadequate support for new demands or foster isolation and competition will undermine motivation and well-being. Practical initiatives include:

  • workload caps and transparent allocation models;
  • responsible-metrics policies that limit reliance on narrow quantitative indicators;
  • recognition and reward of teaching and service;
  • secure contracts and transparent career pathways for contingent staff;
  • mental-health support;
  • policies on digital connectivity that respect boundaries between work and private life.

Figure 4 integrates these strategies within a framework adapted from the JD-R model. Job demands drive a health-impairment process, while job and personal resources drive a motivational process and buffer the effects of demands. Academic resilience is a mediating capacity that attenuates strain and amplifies engagement. Individual, leadership and institutional levers strengthen it. Table 4 maps each major challenge onto its characteristic manifestations and onto corresponding individual and institutional strategies. It thereby provides a practical framework for diagnosing and responding to pressures on academic well-being.

Section 4: The Future of Academic Identity and Institutional Excellence

4.1 The Institution as a Source of Innovation and Ethical Scholarship

The analysis so far has emphasised the ways in which institutions structure and constrain academic identity. Institutions are not merely sources of pressure, however. They are also the primary contexts in which academic identities can be sustained, enriched and renewed. The question for institutional leaders is how to configure institutional structures so that they enable academics to be flexible, creative and effective in high-quality teaching and research. This subsection identifies four institutional commitments that are fundamental to this goal: innovation, academic freedom, ethical scholarship and fair career progression.

Innovation in higher education depends on the willingness of academics to experiment with new forms of teaching, research and engagement. Experimentation entails risk, and academics will take risks only when institutional cultures tolerate failure, reward innovation and provide resources for development. Institutions can act as catalysts for innovation by:

  • establishing teaching and learning centres;
  • funding pedagogical and research innovation projects;
  • creating interdisciplinary spaces;
  • supporting faculty learning communities [24];
  • recognising innovation in appraisal and promotion.

The networked conception of faculty development identified by Sorcinelli and colleagues positions development as a strategic institutional function connected to innovation, rather than a peripheral support service [18].

Academic freedom is the foundation of scholarly identity. Freedom to inquire, to teach according to one's professional judgement, to publish findings and to participate in institutional governance is what distinguishes the academic profession from other forms of knowledge work. Henkel's analysis showed that academic autonomy has been reconfigured rather than abolished [12]. However, metric-driven accountability, commercial pressures and political interference can erode the substance of academic freedom while preserving its form. Institutions that are committed to academic freedom protect academics' discretion over the content and methods of their work. They resist the reduction of academic value to quantitative indicators, and they defend academics who engage in controversial or critical scholarship.

Ethical scholarship is the third commitment. The pressures of performativity and productivity create incentives for questionable research practices, including data fabrication, plagiarism, duplicate publication, honorary authorship and the use of predatory outlets [13,14]. Generative AI introduces new ethical questions concerning authorship, transparency and the integrity of assessment and research [28]. Institutions sustain ethical scholarship through research-integrity policies and training, effective ethics review, clear guidance on the responsible use of AI, and, crucially, by ensuring that their own incentive structures do not reward unethical behaviour. Ethical scholarship is thus an institutional as well as an individual responsibility.

Fair career progression is the fourth commitment. Academics' sense of identity and commitment depends on the perception that recognition and advancement are distributed fairly. Fairness requires transparent and consistently applied criteria and recognition of the full range of academic contributions, including teaching, engagement, leadership and development [7]. It also requires attention to structural inequalities affecting women, academics from marginalised communities and contingent staff [17]. In the Indian context, the career-advancement criteria established by the University Grants Commission [16] provide a structured framework. Their contribution to fairness depends on how they are interpreted and implemented, and on whether they recognise innovation in teaching and engagement as well as research output. The aspirations of the National Education Policy 2020 for merit-based career management and faculty empowerment [15] can only be realised if these commitments are embedded in institutional practice.

These four commitments are mutually reinforcing. Innovation requires the security provided by academic freedom and fair career progression. Ethical scholarship requires incentive structures that do not reward misconduct. Fair progression requires that diverse forms of academic work, including innovative teaching and engagement, are recognised. When institutions honour these commitments, they create the conditions in which academics can sustain identities that are flexible without being fragmented, and committed without being exploited. Referring back to Figure 2, institutional commitment of this kind widens the space for agency at the institutional layer of the ecological model. It thereby shifts the likely outcomes of identity negotiation from strategic compliance and exit toward alignment and creative reinvention.

4.2 Sustained Professional Learning as the Key to Transformation

The chapter's final argument is that sustained professional learning is the cornerstone for supporting academic identity and enabling institutional transformation. This claim follows from the analysis in the preceding sections. If academic identity is fluid and continuously negotiated (Section 1), then academics require ongoing opportunities to develop the knowledge, skills and dispositions that new configurations of identity demand. If the effectiveness of CPD depends on duration, collaboration and integration with practice (Section 2), then episodic training cannot meet this need. If systemic pressures threaten well-being (Section 3), then professional learning must itself be designed as a resource that buffers demands, not an additional demand. If institutions are to be sources of innovation and ethical scholarship (Section 4.1), then they must invest in the professional learning of their staff as a strategic priority.

Four emerging developments, examined in Section 2.2, constitute the building blocks of a future-oriented system of sustained professional learning.

Competency-based professional learning provides a framework for defining the capabilities required for contemporary academic practice, for personalising development pathways, and for assessing attainment through evidence of practice. It moves professional development from an input-based model of hours attended toward an outcome-based model of capability demonstrated.

Global research and teaching networks extend professional learning beyond institutional boundaries. They connect academics with peers across institutions and countries and enable participation in collaborative inquiry at scale [10]. For academics in resource-constrained contexts, such networks offer access to expertise and opportunities that local institutions cannot provide.

AI-supported teaching is both a domain of new competence and a resource for professional learning. Used critically and ethically, AI tools can support the design of learning, the provision of feedback and the analysis of practice. They can thereby enhance academics' capacity for reflective improvement [27,28].

Micro-credentialing provides a mechanism for recognising granular, portable and stackable learning [29,30]. Where micro-credentials are rigorously quality-assured and integrated into career-advancement frameworks, they can make professional learning visible and valued. They can also support mobility across institutions and systems.

Taken together, these developments point toward a model of professional learning that is continuous rather than episodic, personalised rather than uniform, collaborative rather than isolated, recognised rather than invisible, and integrated with practice rather than detached from it. This model corresponds to the integrated CPD ecosystem depicted in Figure 3, with competency frameworks defining the content of learning pathways, networks and AI tools extending their reach, and micro-credentials providing the recognition mechanism. It also addresses the challenges mapped in Table 4 by positioning professional learning as a job resource that supports autonomy, competence and relatedness [36], not as a compliance requirement.

Translating this model into institutional practice requires a staged implementation strategy. In the first stage, institutions should audit existing development provision, appraisal criteria and workload models to identify misalignments between stated priorities and actual incentives. In the second stage, they should articulate a competency framework through participatory processes involving academics at different career stages and in different roles, so that the framework reflects the diversity of academic identity described in Section 1. This framework can draw on the domains summarised in Table 3. In the third stage, they should build the infrastructure of sustained learning: protected time, learning communities, mentoring networks, digital and AI learning environments, and quality-assured micro-credentials. In the fourth stage, they should integrate recognised learning into appraisal and career advancement, and evaluate the effects of the system on practice, well-being and student learning [21]. Each stage depends on leadership that treats professional learning as a strategic investment rather than a cost, and on governance arrangements that give academics a genuine voice in the design of the system that shapes their professional lives.

Two cautions are necessary. First, the developments described here are not panaceas. Competency frameworks risk reducing the richness of academic practice to checklists. Global networks can reproduce existing hierarchies of prestige. AI tools raise unresolved ethical questions. Micro-credentials can degenerate into credentialism. Each requires critical, values-based implementation guided by the purposes of higher education rather than by technological or market logics. Second, professional learning cannot compensate for structural problems such as excessive workload, insecure employment and distorted incentives. Sustained professional learning is the key to transformation only when it is accompanied by the institutional commitments described in Section 4.1. These are reasonable workloads, secure employment, fair appraisal, academic freedom and ethical governance.

The vision of "higher education beyond boundaries" that frames this volume can be articulated in terms of academic identity. It is a vision of academics who can cross the boundaries of discipline, institution, nation and mode of delivery while sustaining a coherent sense of scholarly purpose. Such academics would be equipped through sustained professional learning to engage with digital and AI-mediated environments critically and creatively. They would be supported by institutions that value their full range of contributions and protect the conditions of free, ethical and high-quality scholarship. Realising this vision is a collective project, requiring the commitment of individual academics, academic developers, institutional leaders and policy makers.

Conclusion

This chapter has argued that academic identity in contemporary higher education is a fluid, relational and negotiated construct. It is formed across multiple role domains and shaped by forces operating at the individual, disciplinary, institutional, national and global levels. The chapter makes five main contributions.

  1. A multidimensional model of fluid academic identity (Figure 1; Table 1) identifies the role domains, practices, identity markers and transformative pressures that constitute contemporary academic selfhood.
  2. An ecological model of the forces shaping identity (Figure 2) frames identity formation as a negotiation between systemic pressure and personal agency, and locates the levers through which institutions and policy makers can widen the space for agency.
  3. An integrated CPD ecosystem (Figure 3; Table 2) and a framework of emerging competencies (Table 3) synthesise the evidence on effective professional development and translate it into design principles for future-ready academic practice. The emerging competencies include online pedagogy, AI-supported education, interdisciplinary knowledge and cross-border mobility.
  4. A demands–resources–resilience framework (Figure 4; Table 4) explains how systemic pressures threaten well-being and identifies individual, leadership and institutional strategies for sustaining resilience.
  5. The chapter has argued that institutional commitment to innovation, academic freedom, ethical scholarship and fair career progression, combined with sustained professional learning, is the foundation on which academic identity and institutional excellence can be aligned.

These frameworks are conceptual and integrative and require empirical investigation. Three lines of research are particularly needed.

  • Longitudinal studies of academic identity formation in systems undergoing major policy reform, including Indian higher education under the National Education Policy 2020.
  • Rigorous evaluations of the impact of competency-based CPD, micro-credentials and AI-supported professional learning on teaching practice and student learning.
  • Studies of the institutional conditions under which professional learning functions as a resource rather than a demand.

For practitioners and leaders, the chapter offers a set of tools for diagnosing the pressures on academic identity and for designing professional learning systems that support academics in becoming flexible, creative, ethical and resilient professionals in higher education beyond boundaries.
